title: Modified radical neck dissection
text: Modified radical neck dissection, levels one to five. In this film we follow the operation step by step on a three dimensional model of the left side of the neck, and look closely at the structures that must be preserved: the accessory nerve, the hypoglossal and vagus nerves, the marginal mandibular nerve, the phrenic nerve and brachial plexus, the sympathetic trunk, and the thoracic duct.

title: Position and incision
text: The patient lies supine with a shoulder roll, the neck extended and the head turned to the opposite side. A skin crease incision, such as an apron, or a transverse incision with a vertical limb, gives access from the mandible down to the clavicle, and from the midline back to trapezius. Flap corners are kept away from the carotid artery.

title: Subplatysmal flaps
text: Flaps are raised just deep to platysma: up to the lower border of the mandible, down to the clavicle, back to the anterior border of trapezius, and forward to the midline. The external jugular vein and the great auricular nerve are left on sternocleidomastoid, and the marginal mandibular nerve is protected in the upper flap.

title: Level one
text: Level one is cleared first. The submental triangle is emptied between the anterior bellies of digastric, and then the submandibular triangle, together with the gland. The marginal mandibular nerve is protected, the facial vessels are ligated, and the lingual and hypoglossal nerves are identified deep to mylohyoid.

title: Unwrap sternocleidomastoid
text: The fascia along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid is incised and peeled off the muscle from front to back, as far as its posterior border, staying attached to the specimen. The muscle is then retracted, exposing the carotid sheath and levels two to four.

title: Accessory nerve and level two
text: The posterior belly of digastric is retracted upwards, and the accessory nerve is found crossing the internal jugular vein, then followed to sternocleidomastoid. Level two B is dissected from under the nerve and passed beneath it to join level two A. The hypoglossal nerve, crossing the carotid arteries, marks the upper limit.

title: Posterior triangle, level five
text: In the posterior triangle, the accessory nerve is found about one centimetre above Erb's point, at the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid, and followed down to trapezius. Level five is cleared from the anterior border of trapezius forwards, staying on the prevertebral fascia over splenius, levator scapulae and the scalenes. Cervical plexus branches are divided superficial and lateral to the phrenic nerve.

title: Floor of the neck
text: The specimen is swept forwards over scalenus anterior. The phrenic nerve runs down the front of the muscle, and the brachial plexus emerges behind it, both deep to the prevertebral fascia, which is left intact. The transverse cervical vessels are left on the fascia where possible.

title: Level four and the thoracic duct
text: The lower part of the specimen is divided above the clavicle between clamps and tied. On the left, the thoracic duct arches into the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins at this level. It is ligated rather than cauterised, and a Valsalva manoeuvre is used to check for a chyle leak.

title: Carotid sheath, levels three and two
text: Working upwards, the specimen is peeled off the internal jugular vein, ligating its tributaries, including the common facial vein. The vagus nerve, the common carotid artery and the hypoglossal nerve are kept in view. The specimen is delivered in continuity, haemostasis and chyle are checked, suction drains are placed, and the wound is closed in layers.

title: Structures at risk
text: To summarise, the structures at risk are the accessory nerve, the hypoglossal and vagus nerves, the marginal mandibular nerve, the phrenic nerve and brachial plexus, the sympathetic trunk, and, on the left, the thoracic duct. This film is for education only. Always check surgical detail against current atlases and senior guidance.
